countries.name: Japan
countries.summary: A deep country for regional guessing: road infrastructure, utility poles, plates, reflectors, terrain, climate, and dense visual context all matter.
quick: Short white plates with green text; kei cars can use yellow plates

items.name: Utility-pole plates
items.text: Regional electrical-company plates are one of the strongest foundations for advanced Japan region guessing. The exact plate style varies by region.

items.name: Pole reflectors
items.text: Reflector-pad designs vary by region. Nationwide generic patterns also exist, so the full shape and placement matter.

items.name: Transformers and pole tops
items.text: Transformer mounts, crossbars, and attachments can provide regional information when combined with other pole features.

items.name: Licence plates
items.text: Standard plates are short and light-colored; kei cars commonly use a yellow plate variant. Treat this as supporting context rather than a region clue.

items.name: Road diamonds & signpost stickers
items.text: Some road-diamond styles and signpost stickers are regionally useful, especially at advanced levels.

items.name: Hokkaido pole hardware
items.text: Distinct transformer and pole-top arrangements can strongly support Hokkaido when seen clearly.

items.name: Shikoku & Kansai pole attachments
items.text: Characteristic pole attachments occur in these regions, but examples should be compared carefully before using them as a lock.

countries.name: Ghana
countries.summary: A country with famous coverage clues, clear north–south landscape differences, and useful road/vegetation patterns.
quick: Distinctive Google-car clues on many coverages
Drier savannah north, denser vegetation south

items.name: Ghana tape
items.text: On regular generation-3 road coverage, a roof rack with black tape on the right side of the front bar is a highly distinctive clue.

items.name: Generation-4 pickup
items.text: Generation-4 imagery can show a grey or white pickup with a front antenna, often partly blurred.

items.name: North–south vegetation contrast
items.text: Northern Ghana trends toward drier savannah, while denser forests and palms are more common farther south and southwest.

items.name: Coastal palms
items.text: Tall palms are especially common near parts of the coast and can support a coastal read.

items.name: Black-and-white signposts
items.text: Black-and-white striped signposts are common in Ghanaian cities, but similar patterns exist elsewhere and need supporting context.

countries.name: Colombia

items.name: Yellow licence plates
items.text: Yellow plates are one of Colombia’s strongest visual identifiers in South America when visible clearly.

items.name: Antenna / car context
items.text: Certain generation-3 and generation-4 car appearances can support Colombia, but similar antennas occur elsewhere in the Americas.

items.name: Cross-shaped signpost backs
items.text: White metal signposts often join in a characteristic cross shape behind signs. Similar white posts can occur elsewhere, so inspect the construction.

countries.name: Guatemala

items.name: Guatemala car

items.name: Pastel masonry + sheet-metal roofs
items.text: A common architectural texture, especially useful when combined with terrain, road quality, and the Google car.

items.name: Lake Atitlán landscape
items.text: A large highland lake surrounded by steep mountains and volcanoes creates a distinctive regional environment.

countries.name: Canada
countries.summary: A large country with strong national identifiers and extensive province-level variation in road signs, bollards, utility poles, road numbering, guardrails, and roadside objects.
quick: Metric system; speed signs commonly use “Maximum” and km/h
Provincial licence plates and highway shields
French-language road signs are especially useful in Québec and parts of New Brunswick

items.name: “Maximum” speed-limit signs
items.text: Canadian speed signs use “Maximum” and metric speeds in km/h. US signs generally say “Speed Limit” and use mph; compare wording and number format together.

items.name: Wordless railway and yield signs
items.text: Canadian railway-crossing and yield signs are often symbol-only, while US equivalents more often include wording such as “RAILROAD CROSSING” or “YIELD”.

items.name: Metric units and British English spelling
items.text: Road contexts commonly use kilometres and spellings such as “centre” and “colour”. Useful as supporting evidence against the US, not as a standalone lock.

items.name: Diamond-shaped T-intersection warning sign
items.text: Canada uses a distinctive diamond-shaped T-intersection sign. The guide describes this design as a uniquely Canadian clue; confirm the exact sign shape rather than relying on a generic junction symbol.

items.name: Single versus double yellow centre lines
items.text: Single yellow centre lines are usual in Canada, while double yellow lines are more common in the US. Double lines still occur in Canada, so this is supporting evidence only.

items.name: Generation 2 coverage
items.text: Gen 2 imagery is relatively common in Canada, particularly rural and remote areas, and much rarer in the US. Look for the large circular car blur and halo-like colour distortion in the sky.

items.name: Generation 3 side-mirror blur
items.text: Canadian Gen 3 side mirrors generally appear as two peaks, while US examples more often appear as a single peak. Treat this as a coverage-generation-specific comparison.

items.name: Communal mailboxes and Canada Post branding
items.text: Communal mailboxes can occur in Canada and may carry Canada Post’s red logo. They are described as rare in the US, where USPS branding is blue; personal mailboxes remain common in Canada too.

items.name: Provincial licence-plate designs
items.text: Each province has its own plate design, and some remain recognizable when blurred. Front-plate requirements also differ by province. New Brunswick dropped the general front-plate requirement in 2019, while older coverage may still show front plates; Newfoundland and Labrador commercial vehicles require front plates.

items.name: Provincial highway shields
items.text: Highway shield designs vary by province. The green Trans-Canada Highway shield is found across all ten provinces, so it identifies the route system rather than a specific province.

items.name: Provincial kilometre markers
items.text: Kilometre-marker designs vary slightly by province. Ontario markers have a white square at the bottom, described by the guide as distinctive to Ontario.

items.name: Provincial speed-limit sign variants
items.text: Ontario signs may have a black lower panel with “km/h” or “begins”; British Columbia signs may include “km/h” without that black panel; Québec signs may include French wording.

items.name: Alberta cylindrical black-and-white bollard
items.text: A cylindrical bollard with two black bands wrapping around is common in Alberta. Some have a yellow band between the black bands; blue bands are rare around Calgary and green bands rare around Edmonton. The Alberta bands are thinner than those on the similar Northwest Territories design.

items.name: Manitoba black-and-grey bollards
items.text: Manitoba bollards are described as black and grey painted, often with an orange stripe below the grey. Rectangular wooden forms occur farther north. A black-top-only form also appears in Saskatchewan.

items.name: British Columbia thin black-and-white bollard
items.text: BC bollards are thin and slightly curved, with two black bands spaced more widely than on the similar Alberta bollard. They can occur throughout the province.

items.name: Québec guardrail-mounted reflector poles
items.text: Québec has long, thin white poles attached to guardrails, with a red or green reflector at the top.

items.name: Québec fire-hydrant markers
items.text: Yellow fire-hydrant markers may be mounted atop signposts. Québec City markers often have a blue rectangle; markers in Trois-Rivières are distinctly small. Similar markers also occur in Edmundston, New Brunswick.

items.name: Rectangular roadside markers
items.text: Rectangular markers appear along Québec roads and vary in colour. They can rarely occur on urban divided highways in New Brunswick.

items.name: Diamond-shaped roadside markers
items.text: Diamond-shaped markers occur along Ontario roads; their colours vary.

items.name: Red-and-white chevrons
items.text: Québec is described as the only Canadian province using red-and-white chevrons; elsewhere in Canada, yellow-and-black chevrons are used.

items.name: Transformer orientation relative to the road
items.text: Transformers face the road in British Columbia and New Brunswick; in other provinces they are generally parallel to the wires. In Prince Edward Island and Nova Scotia, transformers are often installed at a 45-degree angle to the road. PEI units often have red numbers on the side.

items.name: Insulator orientation
items.text: Insulators facing toward or away from the road are mostly found in Québec, Nova Scotia and Prince Edward Island. Other provinces more often have insulators facing in the same direction as the road. Avoid using this at intersections or driveways.

items.name: Ontario-style three-insulator pole tops
items.text: A distinctive arrangement has two side insulators and one on top, with characteristic side attachments. Multiple units may be stacked. It can occasionally occur in British Columbia, Nova Scotia and elsewhere.

items.name: Québec black-and-yellow pole label
items.text: Some Québec poles carry a vertical black-and-yellow label with a small “Q” in the black portion.

items.name: Prince Edward Island pole sticker
items.text: Poles on PEI usually feature a small white sticker.

items.name: Alternating Saskatchewan pole insulators
items.text: Adjacent poles may alternate between one insulator on the left and two on the right, then two on the left and one on the right. This pattern can rarely appear in Manitoba.

items.name: Two hanging pole insulators
items.text: Poles with two hanging insulators are common in Manitoba.

items.name: Québec T-intersection sign variant
items.text: Québec T-intersection signs do not feature the chequerboard pattern described for the Canadian design.

items.name: Newfoundland and Labrador T-intersection sign border
items.text: T-intersection signs feature a rectangular yellow border around the diamond shape.

items.name: Green-backed road signs
items.text: Road signs in British Columbia can have green backsides. Green backsides are also somewhat common on Prince Edward Island.

items.name: Hanging sign installation
items.text: Some British Columbia road signs are hung down from distinctive signposts.

items.name: Green-and-white striped signpost sticker
items.text: A green-and-white striped sticker can sometimes be found on signposts in Manitoba.

items.name: White triangles on signposts
items.text: Saskatchewan signposts can feature white triangles; the number of triangles can vary.

items.name: Arrêt-only stop signs
items.text: Stop signs reading “Arrêt” are characteristic of Québec. French is also spoken in minority communities elsewhere, so inspect the exact sign and wider context.

items.name: Bilingual Stop / Arrêt signs
items.text: Stop signs displaying both “Stop” and “Arrêt” are most common in New Brunswick but can rarely occur in other provinces.

items.name: Bilingual street signs
items.text: Street signs in New Brunswick are bilingual. Bilingual street signs also occur in other Canadian areas with French-speaking minorities.

items.name: Alberta Township and Range road grid
items.text: Township roads (Twp Rd) run east–west and their numbers increase northward. Range roads (Rge Rd) run north–south and their numbers increase westward; numbering resets in several places. The guide’s grid infographic multiplies displayed grid numbers by ten to obtain road numbers.

items.name: Manitoba rural road-number grid
items.text: Rural roads are arranged in a grid. Roads ending in N run east–west and their numbers increase by one per mile north of the US border. Roads marked E or W run north–south and indicate position relative to the principal meridian just west of Winnipeg.

sections.title: Guardrails, road markings & other roadside clues

items.name: Concrete highway barriers
items.text: British Columbia predominantly uses concrete barriers instead of guardrails.

items.name: Wire-style highway guardrail
items.text: A guardrail made from small posts connected by three or four metal wires can rarely be found on major Alberta highways.

items.name: Ontario wooden-post wire guardrail
items.text: Ontario often has guardrails made from cylindrical wooden posts joined by exactly three metal wires. Some posts carry a reflective white band.

items.name: Pyramid-topped wooden guardrail posts
items.text: Many wooden guardrail posts have pyramid-shaped tops. Similar tops can occasionally appear on standalone posts and signposts.

items.name: Diamond marker beside fire hydrants
items.text: Fire hydrants often have a diamond-shaped marker beside them.

items.name: Wooden sign-support boxes
items.text: Wooden boxes supporting signs can be found in Newfoundland and Labrador.

items.name: Double yellow centre lines in Eastern Canada
items.text: Within Eastern Canada, double yellow lines are most common in Nova Scotia, followed by Québec and PEI. Ontario generally prefers single yellow lines but sometimes uses double lines.

items.name: White dashes between yellow centre lines
items.text: White dashes can sometimes appear between the yellow centre lines in Saskatchewan.

items.name: Centre-line rumble strips
items.text: Rumble strips in the centre of the road, generally over the road lines, are most common in Alberta and British Columbia.

items.name: Orange-and-black traffic cones
items.text: Ontario uses distinctive orange-and-black striped traffic cones.

items.name: Orange-and-white traffic cones
items.text: Québec uses distinctive orange-and-white striped traffic cones.

items.name: Rectangular street-lamp heads
items.text: Rectangular lampheads are common in New Brunswick and Nova Scotia.

items.name: Short curved utility-pole lamp arms
items.text: Lamp arms on Nova Scotia utility poles are usually curved and much shorter than elsewhere in Canada. Short arms can occasionally occur in other provinces.

items.name: Wooden plank driveway bins
items.text: Wooden plank bins can be seen on Newfoundland driveways. They are most often octagonal but can have other shapes; occasional examples occur in New Brunswick.

confusions.shared: Wooden utility poles, cylindrical transformers, short licence plates, overhead traffic-light bars, water towers, and many road conventions
confusions.distinguish: “Maximum” versus “Speed Limit”, metric versus imperial units, diamond T-intersection signs, Canadian coverage-generation patterns, communal mailboxes, and province-specific infrastructure

confusions.shared: Many bollards, pole fittings, sign designs, and road markings cross provincial borders or occur as rare exceptions
confusions.distinguish: Use combinations of licence plates, highway shields, kilometre markers, utility hardware, road numbering, language, and landscape; avoid single-clue province locks
